summary: This informational RFC describes the role of the chair of the Internet Research Task Force (IRTF), discusses the duties, and outlines the skills an ideal candidate should have.

plainLanguage.summary: A job description for the person who leads a group that studies long-term ideas for the Internet. It says what they do and what skills help.

questions: what does the irtf chair do
subtitle: Job description and expectations for the IRTF chair

tldr.problem: The IRTF Chair role combines strategic research leadership, administrative responsibility, and IAB participation, but the specific expectations and skill set had not been clearly documented.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC outlines the chair's duties in three areas: strategic decisions about which research groups to charter or close, administrative tasks like document review and meeting organization, and participation in the IAB as an ex officio member.
tldr.outcome: The role requires deep involvement in both academic research and operations communities, strong organizational skills, and ongoing time commitments including attendance at IETF meetings.

today: RFC 7827 is a current informational resource for candidates considering or preparing for the IRTF Chair role. It has not been obsoleted and provides the definitive job description for the position. The role continues to require the expertise and commitment described in the RFC.

sections.title: The Role and Scope
sections.content:
The Internet Research Task Force (IRTF) focuses on longer-term research issues related to the Internet, complementing the short-term engineering focus of the IETF. The IRTF consists of Research Groups (RGs) that work on topics including protocols, applications, architecture, and Internet technology. Unlike IETF working groups where organizations send representatives, IRTF RGs attract individual researchers who can commit to stable, long-term collaboration.

The IRTF Chair is appointed by the Internet Architecture Board (IAB) for two-year terms and manages the IRTF in consultation with the Internet Research Steering Group (IRSG). The Chair also serves as an ex officio member of the IAB, bringing research perspective to architectural decisions. This document details the duties of the role and the expertise candidates should have.
sections.plainLanguage: The IRTF studies the Internet's long-term future. Its leader makes decisions about which research topics to pursue and helps connect academic researchers with the engineers building today's Internet.

sections.title: Strategic Leadership
sections.content:
The most important part of the IRTF Chair role is strategic: deciding which Research Groups to charter, which to close, and what new areas the IRTF should explore. Sometimes researchers bring proposals to the Chair, but often the Chair proactively identifies important research areas and motivates the community to form a group.

To excel at this, the Chair must be deeply embedded in both academic research and operational engineering communities. A publication record, membership on conference committees, participation in research projects, and a network of contacts in both worlds are essential. Without these connections, the Chair cannot identify which emerging research matters for the Internet or who the right leaders and participants are.

The Chair also decides when to close Research Groups that have lost momentum, address obsolete topics, or are dysfunctional. This requires strong people skills and clear communication. The Chair manages the Applied Networking Research Prize (ANRP), a joint award with the Internet Society that recognizes outstanding applied research. Running the ANRP selection committee requires knowledge of what constitutes good research and strong ties to the academic community to identify qualified committee members and encourage high-quality nominations.
sections.plainLanguage: The Chair picks which research topics the IRTF should study and finds the right people to lead them. They know both the university researchers and the Internet engineers, so they can spot ideas that matter and bring in the right people to explore them.

sections.title: Administrative and IAB Duties
sections.content:
The IRTF Chair oversees many administrative functions, though some can be delegated to IRSG members. The Chair ensures IRTF documents published as RFCs are high quality, schedules IESG review, and manages publication processes with the RFC Editor and IANA. The Chair approves meeting time slots for RGs at IETF meetings, maintains the IRTF website, and monitors the IETF Datatracker to ensure IRTF documents are accurately tracked.

The Chair appoints and manages RG chairs and IRSG members, and stays informed about research group progress. The Chair also defines IRTF operational procedures (within boundaries set by RFC 2014), handles policy questions on intellectual property, consensus, copyright, and plagiarism, and organizes the IRSG working dinner and the IRTF Open Meeting at each IETF.

The Chair provides monthly status reports to the IAB and writes regular columns for the IETF Journal. These administrative duties resemble those of an IETF Area Director and demand strong organizational and communication skills, regular availability throughout the year, and attendance at most IETF meetings in person plus other related travel.

As an IAB ex officio member, the Chair participates in IAB discussions, attends IAB retreats and workshops, and may shepherd birds-of-a-feather (BoF) sessions to determine whether proposed efforts belong in IETF or IRTF. This requires the same technical and leadership expertise expected of all IAB members.
sections.plainLanguage: Beyond big decisions, the Chair handles paperwork: reviewing documents, organizing meetings, tracking progress, and reporting to leadership. They are always busy and need to attend many in-person meetings. They also sit at the table for big architectural discussions about the Internet's future.

sections.title: Expertise and Commitment
sections.content:
The role requires candidates to have research or academic background, operational management experience, technical leadership, and implementation expertise. Candidates should have served on academic conference program committees and ideally have chaired one, since running the ANRP selection committee is similar to selecting best papers.

The position demands a substantial time commitment throughout the year. Candidates must be willing and able to attend most IETF meetings in person and undertake related travel. The role is not suitable for someone with limited availability or those geographically distant from IETF meeting locations.

Most importantly, candidates need a demonstrated history of participation in both academic research communities and operational engineering communities. Without this bridge between the two worlds, the Chair cannot effectively identify research that matters for real-world Internet deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: The ideal Chair has published research, led people, built software, and stayed connected to both universities and companies. They need to travel constantly and be available year-round. They are a bridge between researchers and operators.
